extracted.intended_audience: general readers and critics interested in opera, theatre, and literary characterisation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critique on opera performance (acting, chorus, scenery, staging) with additional commentary on plausibility and character responsibility in fiction. The page is a literary essay discussing how musical necessity, stagecraft, and realistic behaviour should shape performance and storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composer's primary aim: music above other arts
rubrics_metrics.description: "The object to be aimed at by the wise composer should be to make us, while listening to his music, forgetful of all remaining artistic considerations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that a composer should make the music itself paramount so the listener becomes "forgetful" of other artistic concerns; Wagner's attempt to subsume all arts into music-drama is questioned as impractical. Use music to absorb attention rather than rely on spectacle to replace music's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opera prioritises musical necessity over naturalistic acting
rubrics_metrics.description: "In opera, everything is rightly sacrificed to musical necessity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise that singers must often accept non-naturalistic stage conventions because of vocal demands. Practical implication: staging and movement should be arranged to preserve vocal delivery even if that means sacrificing realistic interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conserve vocal resources through economical stagecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: "The experienced artist takes the centre of the stage and husbands his resources."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Singers should manage their physical effort and blocking to avoid wasting breath or energy (avoid excessive physical embraces, complex choreographies while sustaining demanding singing). Plan centre-stage moments and rest positions to protect the voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impractical physical interactions while singing
rubrics_metrics.description: When singing at the top of your voice you don’t want a heavy woman hanging round your neck... When you are killing a man and warbling about it at the same time, you don’t want him fooling around you defending himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Staging should account for what is physically realistic while accommodating vocal performance: avoid close-contact business that impedes singing, and do not ask performers to perform physically strenuous or realistic combat while delivering demanding vocal lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: turning to the audience to declare feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Operatic convention: the lover puts his sweetheart in a corner, turns his back, comes down to the footlights and tells the audience how he adores her; she then comes down and tells the audience she is mad about him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conventional device is criticised as artificial. While musical form often forces expository solos, directors should be aware this is an operatic convention and, where possible, find ways to make such declarations feel more integrated with believable stage action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting should reflect plausible human reactions in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: If you have been severely wounded... you don’t want to have to think how a man would really behave who knew he had only got a few minutes to live... The chances are that he would not want to sing at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even within the musical constraints, performers and directors should consider how a real person would behave in intense situations (wounds, mob attacks, imminent death) and avoid staging that conflicts egregiously with basic human reactions; seek staging solutions that honour both drama and music.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic crowd/mob behaviour on stage
rubrics_metrics.description: If a mob is climbing the stairs thirsting for your blood, you do not want to stand upright with your arms stretched out... you would push against that door for all you were worth, and yell for somebody to bring you a chest of drawers and a bedstead...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Directors should stage crowd scenes with practical physical responses (pushing, barricading, panicked calls for help) rather than static tableau movement that undermines plausibility, while balancing singers' vocal needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus selection: experience, sobriety, and musical knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great thing required of that operatic chorus is experience... The sober, honest, industrious lady or gentleman, with a knowledge of music is very properly his ideal."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise experienced, disciplined choristers who understand musical demands. Practical advice: avoid overly youthful, giddy performers in the chorus; choose steady performers who can produce unified musical and visual effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus unity in costume and behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: What I admire about the chorus chiefly is its unity. The whole village dresses exactly alike... There is probably a meeting called... The costume to be worn by the ladies will consist of a short pink skirt... bolero in mauve silk...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure coordinated costumes, rehearsed grouping, and pre-arranged presentation so choruses appear as a unified body. Practical staging includes pre-performance meetings to agree on costume and positioning to create the intended pictorial effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scepticism about replacing other arts with music-drama (scenery and statuary)
rubrics_metrics.description: It cannot be done, Herr Wagner, believe me. You cannot substitute the music drama for all the arts combined... I am not quite sure the general public does care for statuary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of claims that opera staging or music-drama can fully replace fine art (painting, sculpture). Spectacular backcloths and grouped singers may entertain, but they are not direct substitutes for paintings or statuary appreciated by connoisseurs; composers/directors should use scenic effects judiciously and not depend on them to supply unrelated artistic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiction: character plausibility and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Why did Faust not marry the girl?... I want her to grasp the fact that after all she is only one of us. I should like her better if, instead of demanding 'What is wrong in civilisation?' she would occasionally say to herself: 'Guess I've made a fool of myself this time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should avoid sentimental or conventional exoneration of characters (particularly women); craft characters who are responsible, self-aware, and plausible in their decisions. Reject the trope that female characters are always blameless victims; show internal acknowledgement of mistakes to increase respect and realism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot plausibility: consider realistic, practical resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: There could have been a garden. Marguerite might have kept chickens and a cow... Faust and Marguerite could have slipped into a church one morning, and have kept [the Devil] out of the way with a sword hilt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing plots, authors should consider practical and plausible alternatives to melodramatic actions. Explore ordinary, believable life-choices (e.g., marriage, domestic arrangements) as viable narrative outcomes rather than defaulting to contrived tragedy without justification.
